A.explanation: About $10^{-7}\text{ m}$ is ultraviolet to visible light, which lies near the middle of the spectrum, not in region Q near the long-wavelength end.

B.explanation: About $10^{-5}\text{ m}$ is infrared radiation, which is only a few steps from the $10^{-10}\text{ m}$ end, not as far to the long-wavelength side as Q.

C.explanation: Region Q is the microwave region, second from the long-wavelength end, with typical wavelength of order $10^{-2}\text{ m}$.

D.explanation: About $10^{0}\text{ m}$ is radio waves, which is the extreme long-wavelength end region to the left of Q.

hints: Notice the arrow says wavelength increasing to the left and $10^{-10}\text{ m}$ is marked at the right-hand end, so the right side is gamma-rays and X-rays.

Recall the typical wavelength order for that named region compared with $10^{-7}\text{ m}$ for visible light and $10^{0}\text{ m}$ for radio waves.
walkthrough: The diagram has seven boxes for the principal regions and wavelength increases to the left, with $10^{-10}\text{ m}$ at the right side for X-rays.
Ordering from short to long wavelength is gamma-rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves.
Region Q is second from the left, with only one longer-wavelength region to its left, so Q is microwaves and the leftmost box is radio waves.
Microwaves are much longer than visible light at about $10^{-7}\text{ m}$ and infrared at about $10^{-5}\text{ m}$, but shorter than radio waves at $10^{0}\text{ m}$ and above.
A typical microwave wavelength is millimetres to centimetres, of order $10^{-3}\text{ m}$ to $10^{-1}\text{ m}$, best matched by $10^{-2}\text{ m}$.
